title: Tempo and dancing versus dazzling listeners
summary: Tempo changes what a player plays; Caldwell dropped his fast Body and Soul; they contrast dance tempos with tempos for listeners at tables.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: How much does tempo affect you? I mean, you know, if you were accustomed to playing a tune like you were playing on the -- at a certain tempo, and somebody hits it off much faster, I mean that changes what you play considerably, doesn't it?

Yes, it does, yeah. Changes the whole aspect of what you want to play, change it all the way around. I used to play (unintelligible) Body and Soul, three or four choruses as a ballad. Then we pick it up in two/four, fast two/four. But I quit doing it. Not that I didn't want to do it, but Charlie Ventura (unintelligible) tell me, he says, come here and listen. Said, why do you play it with the bell (unintelligible) play it in an even swing tempo? And so that's (the way) (unintelligible) wanted to do it. So I just it every night follow suit. But like you say, Stanley, you play the light and it becomes monotonous to you.
Well, that's right. You can't help that. I mean that's impossible, but I think that there's another thing that has changed. You know those tempos used to be --
Those tempos used to be right to make
Well, now you're no longer thinking like that. You're thinking entirely in terms of what will dazzle these people sitting at those tables with their beers.
